explanation_text: On a Zhuangjin (Zhuang brocade) loom, every row holds its own position, and the place where a thread sits decides the design it forms—just as the position of a digit decides its value.
image_prompt: Illustrate a Zhuangjin brocade loom with woven rows labeled as ones, tens, and hundreds, showing how each thread's row position shapes the pattern, like digit places determine value.

explanation_text: At the Sanyuesan festival, cooks add more dyed rice to a bowl and the total grows; when some is served out, the total shrinks—exactly like addition and subtraction.
image_prompt: Show bowls of five-color glutinous rice being filled and emptied, with totals changing as portions are added or removed.

explanation_text: The terraces of Longji march up the hillside in equal rows; counting the terraces in each row is multiplication, and sharing the plots evenly among families is division.
image_prompt: Display equal rows of Longji rice terraces arranged on a hillside, showing equal grouping (multiplication) and even sharing (division).

zhuang_culture: Water buffalo pairs in the field
explanation_text: Water buffalo yoked in pairs for plowing make even numbers; when one buffalo stands alone, the number is odd.
image_prompt: Show water buffalo yoked in pairs in a rice paddy, with one single buffalo standing apart to represent an odd number.

explanation_text: The repeating color stripes woven into a Zhuangjin brocade follow a steady rhythm, like skip counting—every fifth motif marks the same hue.
image_prompt: Show a strip of Zhuangjin brocade with repeating colored motifs, highlighting every fifth pattern to illustrate skip counting.

explanation_text: Comparing how full two bamboo rice baskets are shows which holds more or less, just like comparing numbers with greater than and less than signs.
image_prompt: Show two bamboo baskets holding different amounts of rice, with > and < symbols placed between them.

explanation_text: When making glutinous rice cakes, elders estimate roughly how many cups of rice are needed rather than counting each grain—like rounding to a nearby convenient number.
image_prompt: Show cooks estimating scoops of rice for festival rice cakes, labeling the amounts with rounded numbers.

explanation_text: When a plate of five-color glutinous rice is shared equally among singers at the Sanyuesan festival, each person receives a fraction of the whole plate.
image_prompt: Show a round plate of five-color sticky rice divided into equal servings, each labeled as a fraction of the whole.

explanation_text: Cutting a sweet potato rice cake into 2 equal pieces or into 4 smaller equal pieces gives the same total amount—like equivalent fractions.
image_prompt: Show a round rice cake divided first into halves and then into quarters, demonstrating equal total portions.

explanation_text: Tying several small bundles of rice into one large bundle keeps the harvest the same while the count simplifies—just like reducing a fraction to its lowest terms.
image_prompt: Depict small bundles of rice being gathered into one larger bundle, labeled with the fraction reduced to simplest form.

explanation_text: If a household has 3 full bamboo baskets of rice and half a basket more, that is 3½—exactly a mixed number.
image_prompt: Show three full bamboo rice baskets and one half-full basket labeled as 3½.

explanation_text: When dyed rice spills past one bamboo steamer but is still counted in equal portions, it forms an improper fraction—a value greater than one whole.
image_prompt: Show several small bamboo rice steamers piled beyond one full basket, symbolizing fractions greater than 1.

explanation_text: Mixing portions of red and yellow dyed rice into one bowl shows how fractional amounts join to make a whole.
image_prompt: Show small bowls of differently dyed rice being combined into one full bowl.

zhuang_culture: Serving out part of a rice bowl
explanation_text: Ladling part of the sticky rice out of a bowl leaves a remainder—an example of subtracting a fraction.
image_prompt: Show a bowl of sticky rice with part being scooped out, the remaining amount labeled as the fraction left.

explanation_text: If a family takes half of the harvest from half a terrace, they are finding a fraction of a fraction—like multiplying fractions.
image_prompt: Show a terraced field split in halves, with one half divided again to show a smaller portion of the harvest.

explanation_text: Slicing one sticky rice roll into many equal smaller rolls shows how many times a smaller portion fits into a larger one—dividing fractions.
image_prompt: Show a sticky rice roll cut into equal smaller pieces to illustrate fractional division.

explanation_text: When rice is weighed on a market scale, amounts like 1.5 kilograms mix whole numbers and tenths—introducing decimals.
image_prompt: Show a market scale with bags of rice weighed and labeled 1.0, 1.5, and 2.0 kilograms.

explanation_text: Saying half a basket of rice or 0.5 basket describes the same amount—just like converting between fractions and decimals.

explanation_text: When a student answers 90 of 100 questions correctly on a Zhuang language exam, that is 90 percent—parts per hundred.
